utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Tuesday, December 1st, 2009, and I greet our witness, I greet the accused, the Defence counsel. I also greet Mr. Scott and his case manager, as well as everyone helping him. And I also greet everyone helping us around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, you have some IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 4D and 2D have submitted their objections to the Prosecution's list of documents tendered via Witness 4D-AB. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01134 and 01135 respectively. The Prosecution has also submitted their objections to 2D and 3D lists of documents tendered via Witness 4D-AB. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01136. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before I give the floor to Ms. Alaburic, I have a small question for you. I would like some additional information. When you took office, so far as you remember, could you tell us who was the head of the Main Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I took office, which post do you mean, at the beginning of the war or maybe later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the beginning of the war, when you left the JNA, in 1992. I looked at you here in the Kordic case, and I saw "Mr. Petkovic." Very well, it was Mr. Petkovic. And what month was it when you took office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. I first met him in May. Whether he was chief of the Main Staff, I don't know, but he was the person I communicated with. These were just the beginnings, and he was one of the persons I communicated with, and I realised that he was a person I could communicate with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It was in May, as far as you remember. In the indictment, Mr. Petkovic is chief of the Main Staff as of April 1992, so what you said seems to corroborate, that he was chief of the Main Staff at the time. Thank you. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to greet everybody in the courtroom, and particularly you, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By questioning Mr. Petkovic, we are going to deal with the moment when he took office of chief of the Main Staff, so I'm not going to inquire about that with you. Let's resume where we stopped yesterday, the issue of Busovaca. We promised to produce some maps. I hope that Their Honours received those maps. I propose that we give the witness both maps so that we can save some time. We are going to show the map in connection with the document 4D392. This is dated 18th of January, 1993, the Security Administration of the Staff of the Supreme Command. The last paragraph, which may I remind everybody here, read: "Army of the BiH, in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps or Central Bosnia, can fight the HVO under the condition that they cut off road communications: first of all, Busovaca-Kiseljak-Fojnica at Lugovi and Kacuni; and secondly, the road communication Busovaca-Vitez -- secondly, the road communication Busovaca-Vitez; and, thirdly, the road communication Vitez-Travnik at Mecave." General, you see on the ELMO this document. I can't see what's showing there.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the other map, the other map, please. General, to save time I marked what you did during the proofing for your examination, so let's just see where would be the cutoff point of the first road communication, Busovaca-Kiseljak-Fojnica at Lugovi and Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon. We're not getting -- I don't know about the Judges, but we're not getting any broadcast of what's on the ELMO. We can't follow the testimony or the markings that are being made, so it's a bit difficult for us to -- now we have it. It's not on -- it's not on ours, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I no longer have the image, now the Defence teams do not have the image. Let's not waste time. Let's skip working on the map, since we do not have the technical possibility for that, or maybe we can put it off for a bit. We are going to skip the documents relating to the maps. If things are mended in the meantime, we can revisit the maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now continue with the issue of Busovaca. Let's take a look at 4 -- 2D1206 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, unfortunately we couldn't see the map. Maybe we will have an opportunity to see it later, when the system is up again. There is a question that crops up every week from the Prosecution as well as from the Defence. It's the question of the lines of communications, of the ways of communication, and we're told that there were these corridors, and if the corridor is cut off, then there are consequences. At least that's what we are told, as Judges. And the Prosecution and the Defence is always talking about these consequences. And as we just saw, if the road is cut off, it's impossible to move forward anymore. Now, I'm talking to the servicemen. When you are in a situation when the road is cut off, can't you just bypass it, going through the woods, maybe, or through the mountains, maybe transporting weapons on your back, you know, like the Vietnamese did in the Ho Chi Minh Trail or on bicycles, because, you know, they had bicycles and they were able to carry artillery pieces that way? So in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when roads were cut off, did this really prevent any army, whether it be the HVO or the BH Army, to act? Did it really immobilise these armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many cut-off points, but there were alternative routes for vehicles, and of course say nothing about pedestrians. But those three or four points where communication would be cut off would mean that the person or the side cutting off communication would prevent the other side from gaining access to alternative routes. There were no functional alternatives to those communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You say that there was no alternative route. Fine, I agree with you. But even so, if you go through the mountains or through the woods, can't you just bypass the blockade that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, provided it is not manned. But, first of all, those check-points, those cut-off points, were introduced by allies. These were a psychological blow. Then you start to wonder whether we are allies or not. People cannot travel, they cannot see their physician, go to a hospital. So this cutting off of communication was not just a military ploy. It will add ramifications on the civilian life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are adding an additional element which may be important. You're saying that the fact that allies are cutting off the road has psychological consequences, important psychological consequences, but militarily you could bypass that roadblock as long as the woods or the mountains are not occupied by the enemy. But for you, the most important thing is that it's a psychological blow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both a psychological blow and a military blow. If I'm taking a transport from Kiseljak to Jajce and it encounters check-points very frequently, then communication grinds down to a halt. So one of the main problems were those check-points on roads. These were not just a handful, it was a host of check-points, and we were fighting all along to remove those check-points. First of all, there was a war of plunder, and later on it was ethnical, political, and military. Check-points served the purpose of looting, of taking property away, and very few check-points were set up by the military. They were just set up by officers in the rear along the roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm sure we will revisit this issue later on. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've been told that the ELMO is now working.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, General, please, take a look at the map, first the map concerning the document 4D392. This is the map. So, General, please tell us, in this document by the Army of BiH, it is stated that the road communication Busovaca-Kiseljak-Fojnica should be cut off at Lugovi and Kacuni, as first. Please put "1" by the location Lugovi and number 2 by the location Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, General, under "1" on the map, it doesn't state "Lugovi," it says "Bilalovac." Could you please explain where Lugovi is located?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Lugovi is a settlement close by. It doesn't show because of the fact that the map is not that detailed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. It says "Vitez-Travnik" in the document. It should be cut off at the place Mecave. Please put number 3 by that place.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then it is stated -- for the Busovaca-Vitez road, it doesn't state where it should be cut off. We've placed this dotted line here. Please, General, explain why was it put here?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the place Santici or Ahmici [indicates], and this is the best place to cut off this road. At other places, it's much more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Place "4," please, by that place, and now date the map and sign it.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to get an IC number for this map, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked map shall be given Exhibit IC01137. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next map. It's connected with 4D1208. In the last paragraph of that document, it is stated that: "PAT is relocated from Gornja Visnjica village to the village of Dusina to secure the road between Dusina and Sudine." Please place "1" next to the village of Visnjica, number 2 by the village of Dusina, and number 3 next to the village of Sudine.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, General -- indicate the direction of this PAT.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is transferred from the Bosna River Valley to this place to control the area towards Kacuni or the Busovaca-Vitez communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please place "4" by Kacuni, and date and sign the map, please.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to get an IC number for this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The second marked map shall be given Exhibit IC01138. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's go back to the document which we started our conversation with, 4D1206. It is a report by the commander Dzemal Merdan. In the paragraph entitled "Zenica," in the second sentence it states --

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please give the witness the binder containing the documents of the General Petkovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have it now, but in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now you have it in the B/C/S as well. In the second sentence, General, it is stated: "With the aim of closing down the Dusina-Lasva-Sudine road from elevation 852 to Dusina, we engaged 25 newly-mobilised men, 70 men from the 7th Muslim Brigade, and 20 soldiers of the Anti-Sabotage Detachment." Please specify the place those forces of the Army of BiH are heading towards.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those places are along the left bank of the Lasva, that is to say, opposite Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it in the direction of Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just a moment. Let me take a look. Yes, Dusina-Lasva-Sudine. It's the same direction and access that we marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness be provided with a binder containing the documents. So until we're waiting for that, we're going to skip over a few documents, Your Honours, and take a look at map 4D560, 4D560, which is a schematic, and you'll see it on the monitor, General, of the area of Central Bosnia as of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this map, please, General. One of the axes of action by the BH Army, we have listed here the area around Busovaca. Can you tell us whether Kacuni is within that general area covered by the arrow?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Kacuni. But I can see that the direction towards Bugojno was cut off, but that was in October. Anyway, the arrow does show the place where Kacuni is located.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, as Judge Antonetti asked you about alternative directions and axes, tell us what the width of this blue area is controlled by the Croats at Vitez, for example. How broad is that?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 800 to 900 metres at Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in the Vitez area, moving towards Busovaca, what is the largest width of territory under Croatian control?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The largest width is about two and a half to three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, regarding Dusina at elevation 852, I know this village because I've been there. There was a massacre in this village. Everyone knows about it. Now, whenever an army captures a village, whatever the army, and perpetrates crimes, the army doesn't stay in that area, it moves on. Now, according to you, is it controlling the territory or is it a strategic capture? If it's a strategic capture, you're supposed to stay and hold the territory. But if you just move about after that, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the army takes control of a locality, in principle, there should be no forces coming after it to commit crimes. But in this war of ours, taking control of a place means having control of it, which means that the opposite side, the enemy side, no longer has control or does not have control, but the population stays there with all their frustrations and God knows what from before. And then, in continuation, crimes or the various things that they should not do are done. For example, in 1993 we took Grbavica, and then we saw other people taking away property the next day; civilians, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have answered my question, in part. You're saying when a place is taken over, it's to control it, but does this mean that controlling it does not necessarily involve constant presence of the army? You can take over the place and then move on; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let's look at another map, which is 4D561. It's the same territory, but now with the situation as of March and April 1993. Here we have it. Now, General, this Croatian territory has cut between Busovaca and Kiseljak. Tell us, please, until the end of the war did the Croatian forces manage to establish communication between Kiseljak and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a depth of 12 kilometres, and the area remained cut off between Busovaca and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On this map, General, we see the attack by the BH Army launched in the vicinity of Vitez from the Zenica direction. Now, within that area, is that where the village of Ahmici is located?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. We are finished with the topic of Busovaca now, and cutting off the corridor, and realising the plan to form Croatian enclaves. I'd like to inform the Trial Chamber now that because I spent rather a lot of time yesterday, I have reorganised my examination-in-chief so that now I'm going to deal with Sovici and Doljani, and these are documents to be found in the second binder. And if there's any time left over after we finish discussing that topic, I'll revert back to other areas and topics. Your Honours, we're first of all going to show you a film, or half an hour of it, the beginning of a film, a film by Television Konjic. It is P2187, and it is about a meeting between the representatives of the HVO and BH Army held on the 4th of May, 1993, in Jablanica. You have the transcript. We're showing you this film because we want to paint a portrait of General Milivoj Petkovic, and we consider that it would be very useful if you could hear the speakers speaking in their own tongues, Bosnian, Serbo-Croatian, B/C/S, just so that you can see the tones used by Sefer Halilovic and Arif Pasalic, on the one hand, and General Petkovic, on the other. That's the purpose of us showing you this film. Thank you. So let's look at that now, let's watch it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, were you at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm the main person there sitting to the left of Petkovic. I was there as one of the main people in the Joint Command. Delic is sitting here, Sefer and others. Perhaps you didn't notice them, but I did. They're there. And in Zenica, I was shown the command that would be a joint command, and then with Delic and Sefer and the others, and with UNPROFOR, we moved to the Konjic area. I spent the night there with them, or, rather, two nights in Konjic, in those caves there, and then came to this meeting. And I was absolutely astounded to see the atmosphere prevailing at the meeting, because I was in all that commotion -- all those commotions and so on. This was a continuation of the previous relationships, allowing the people behind there to shout and behave in that general way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, since you're describing the atmosphere in that way, are you describing the conduct of the president of the HVO or the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how the BH Army behaved, or the Muslims ultimately, because we were in Jablanica, they controlled Jablanica. There were no Croats there. Well, there were 150 metres away. In a museum or somewhere, there were over 100 persons incarcerated down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, did General Petkovic demonstrate readiness for co-operation? What was your impression about his real intentions and wishes?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our side, on the whole, as a whole, wanted, wished, and endeavoured to do that. Well, if it was Bosnia-Herzegovina, you couldn't have somebody else try to appropriate Bosnia-Herzegovina and exclude me, for example, when you have statehood. But in this particular case, and this has jogged my memory, it was absolutely a flagrant example. A state was being destroyed, they're slaughtering us, slitting our throats, but it's all a pose. First of all, there were organised meetings by the international community, UNPROFOR in actual fact, so the UNPROFOR commanders were there, but -- well, the European Monitors, too, observers. So this was just play-acting for representatives of the international community. They repeated "the republic," "we," "we are the legal ones, we're the real ones, and you are," everything else, all the rest of it, which according to the Goebbels model, when he said that a lie repeated 100 times becomes the truth. So in international relations and overall relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, it became evident that the green flag was the main flag, the official flag. That was what was being portrayed, and that my tricolour was of no value at all, that I wasn't in Bosnia at all. So this meeting showed the culmination point of relations of this kind. Now, the question was: What was Petkovic like? Well, in my opinion, he was too calm, faced with the events that were discussed at that meeting. I suppose that he was able to restrain himself, and you could see that demonstrated at this meeting. So he was calm and he believed that he should work consistently to achieve his aim; first of all, to avoid a conflict and to have conflicts resolved, and to start setting up a Bosnia-Herzegovina in the best way possible for the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only for one nation, for one ethnicity there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We heard at this meeting, General, that Mr. Petkovic said, discussing Mostar, Let's make Mostar an open city, and Mostar will be the way that Mostar people want it to be. According to your knowledge at the time, would you tell us whether this was the frank and earnest attitude of the Croats of the time and as expressed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left an area where I'd been for a year in very shaky circumstances to go and resolve problems. I was not familiar in detail with this situation in Mostar, or in Jablanica, or in Konjic. I was just getting to know the facts. And in my example and in Petkovic's example, you had to attend hundreds of meetings to make some progress, and risk your life in the process, and the overall attitude of the Croatian side, and Petkovic as being at the head of the armed forces, was we were pro co-operation. We wanted to resolve problems and allow everybody to live.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at some details concerning Sovici and Doljani. You have the documents, and I would like to ask Madam Usher to help the witness find the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we move on to Sovici, I, like all the other Judges, have watched this video very carefully, and in this footage we saw Mr. Halilovic, Mr. Petkovic. You, yourself, were there, so was Pasalic, and then there's the Spaniard presiding over the meeting. And watching and listening to the footage, I was very impressed by the tone of all those who took part. Mr. Halilovic was very firm in the way he spoke, and Mr. Petkovic really is very moderate and he tries to open the way for movement on the ground. He offers to Mr. Halilovic to go straight to Doljani, to go with him to Mostar, and each side blames the other for responsibility to some degree. And the background to all this has been set by Halilovic, when he asked General Petkovic whether he was a friend or a foe. And depending on the answers, he will adjust his position, together with a threat of an all-out conflict. So any Judge watching this video footage is rather impressed by the will of each side that addresses obvious facts; arrest, people being driven out, and all that. And I'm also surprised by the fact that on several occasions, General Petkovic told General Halilovic that he should give him lists for checks, and for people to be released immediately, or for them to be able to go back home straight away. So there seems to be goodwill on both sides. But if you watch this footage, you think, well, what is the Spaniard doing? He could have taken hold of the dialogue, controlled it, but he didn't say a thing. How do you account for that? Is it because he had to remain neutral whilst he's in front of two individuals who are willing to enter into a dialogue? So it seemed as though it was possible to find a solution easily, but in this footage the Spaniard does not say a single word. How do you account for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Sefer Halilovic and others, and the audience sitting at the back, attacked us so much that I personally felt threatened, and I accepted to be shot at any moment. This was the general climate. But it wasn't for the first time, so in a way we had gotten used to that. Throughout that meeting, there were attacks against the HVO. We were blamed for everything. We were blamed for being alive. That was the general atmosphere. If you ask me about the Spanish Battalion, the person chaired the meeting as long as he could, and you could see that in the first half of the movie. Later on, he could not chair the meeting, and Sefer Halilovic could not control his brigade's commander to keep his attitude in check during such a meeting. Generally, at such meetings, for instance, at one meeting in Konjic some two or three days later, there was this local commander, Zuka, who burst into the meeting and hugs Cibo on the other side, and he said, We've resolved the issue of Vrce. For me, it was an international meeting at the top level, and you have some local commander bursting in and kissing one attendee and saying that he'd resolved the Vrce issue. What had they done? They'd liquidated the HVO in the Vrce village, and that was three days after the meeting with Sefer Halilovic that we saw on the film, maybe four days later. So in terms of frankness, the possibility of resolving problems and issues, on the Croatian side, on the part of the HVO, realising that we had to fight for our positions in different ways, both through negotiations, which we did all along, but we continuously were battered. In terms that the international community could not help us, well, they could not help the other sides either. They could only be mediators. The Spaniards were in the same position as other units of UNPROFOR, as far as I could tell where I attended meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, at the very beginning of the meeting, the Spaniard said, in his language, We're going to work for peace, "Vamos a trabajar por la paz para." Very good, but apparently General Petkovic and General Halilovic are along that line. But if they're all working towards peace, what does SpaBat do? Is it totally neutral? That's what I wanted to know from you. Why did SpaBat not take over the situation and try to control it, because technically it seemed a rather easy thing to do, given the commitment displayed by all sides. So how do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you are forcing me into an awkward situation. In terms of the quality of the armies that I had contact with, the British, the French, the Nordic people, and the Dutch people, you could rely on them; the Dutch to a lesser extent. As far as the other forces were concerned, you could hardly rely on whether to attend those meetings or not, because they were not ready and equipped and trained for critical situations, in my opinion, and critical situations are foreseeable and possible. In this concrete example, the Spanish Battalion was far from -- particularly when new units would come in - they had a tour of duty of six months - they could not find their bearings. But at that meeting, I was taken aback by the atmosphere and the mode of work. And, after all, the Spanish Battalion were also threatened, they were also in jeopardy. Let's not be fooled to think that UNPROFOR and European Monitors did not risk their lives. They were threatened as well. They were sitting ducks at times between two sides in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But that may be one more reason to get more involved, because if you go by this footage, this can be sort of a very animated discussion, but we've all been part of much harder meetings, and it did not seem impossible to find common ground between all sides. That's the impression I gathered from this footage, and I was seeking your impression. And in answering my question, you said that SpaBat did not really seem to be up to the task, which may be true. But, sir, following this meeting, did General Halilovic and General Petkovic go together on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they did go in SpaBat APCs to the area of Sovici and Doljani. I, with another group, were supposed to go to Konjic, and a third group was supposed to go to Kostajnica. However, the other two groups could not go through -- at least my group could not on that day, allegedly because of a check-point. And, you see, when you're sitting in an APC, you may be sitting for hours, not knowing what's going on. But I do know that that group visited Sovici and Doljani. Well, for me, toponyms and the people in that area were unknown to me. There were hundreds of people, hundreds of toponyms. I tried to get to know brigade commanders, battalion commanders, the names of places, as far as I could, so that in my capacity as a member of the Joint Command, to function and to perform my duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since we were speaking about Doljani and Sovici, Ms. Alaburic wanted to address these issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us, when you visited the ground on the 4th of May in those different groups, where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the preceding two nights I spent in Konjic, which was completely under the control of the ABiH, and I think that that night I slept in Capljina with family that I saw for the first time after several months. I think it was either that or the next day, the 5th of May, because there was another meeting later on. At Capljina, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And I'm interested in the 5th of May meeting. Please, Your Honours, in the other binder, and for the witness in the penultimate set of documents, there must be a book-mark. There is a document P2200. General, it's a very brief document. You may rely on e-court to peruse it. The document is P2200, in the penultimate set of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, I had to reshuffle the sequence of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, if you could bring the binder to me, I will find the document for her [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us, have you ever seen this brief memo before?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it during the proofing meeting in the past two or three days while being primed for this examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who is the author of this memo?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a query addressed to a unit concerning Sovici and Doljani, but it, in effect, is a fruit of my intervention. In other words, Petkovic and Halilovic spoke, and Petkovic asked me to inquire about the buses for Doljani and Sovici, and I did not know anything about Doljani and Sovici, or any other buses. But to cut a long story short, I established contact with the Main Staff, and they tell me -- or, rather, the duty officer -- well, I had to explain that there was an agreement that we would provide the buses to transport the greens. So who, what? And then I said, Well, to transport the greens. I was, in essence, the author of this inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, when you said "the greens," who did you mean?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the Muslim side, because otherwise -- in our communications and in my way of thinking, villages with green flags, denoted in the green colour, that was the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, with this word "green" or "greens," did you wish to under-rate the Muslim population in any way by using that word?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't under -rate something that is there, that I grew up with, and that was the majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, was it your intention, tell us, to belittle them? Was it supposed to be a sort of insult, insulting word for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the area that I came from, for the Serbs and Muslims and Croats, there are derogatory terms, and in this case that would be "balija," but that was not it. It was just a way of denoting who it might concern. And in wartime, in general, I try not to insult anyone. It was the duty officer down there, in talking to me - it couldn't have been otherwise than that - he included the word, but it wasn't derogatory. They were under a green flag. So I don't see where the problem is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, did you receive a response? Had the buses been dispatched or not?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received oral information that the buses had been sent. Well, this is the gist of it, that the buses were from Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "That there were buses, I know that from Arif Pasalic," interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, 4D477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, regarding this question of the greens, according to the Prosecution this means that you looked at the Muslims as people who might be potential victims. Ms. Alaburic is asking you to give more details about who those greens are. Now, I would like to know the following: On your military maps, when you were meeting together with your officers, did the Muslims use green markers?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you use green markers and green flags to symbolise the Muslims? Did the greens represent the enemy, the Muslims? Without any derogatory meaning behind this, as you would say, the reds, the blacks, the whites, did you use those just to say who they were, militarily-wise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the JNA, you had the red was JNA and the enemy was the blue. Now, as far as I was concerned, I had a bit of a problem because we used red to denote the Serbs, the colour blue for the HVO, and the green was for the Muslim forces, not in attack and defence; but deployment and so on, their positions and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that. Now, in your document, because you told us that you wrote this document, you are asking a question about the population. You seem to be surprised about the fact that they were in Sovici and Doljani, and you were wondering where they came from. According to you, there weren't supposed to be any civilians present there, and you were told that they had to be evacuated and you were very surprised? Is that why you put this question in your text about these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. At meetings, and you just saw an excerpt from one such meeting, the footage we were shown, there's the official part and then there are talks and meetings, waiting for APCs or whatever, this interim period. And at one of these sort of interim periods, Petkovic was talking to Sefer, or Sefer talking to Petkovic, and then Petkovic came up to me and said, Have this checked out, check and see if the buses have been sent to Sovici and Doljani. And then he left. Now, had he asked me that in Bosnia, that's where I was fighting and that would have been easy, but all these toponyms, Sovici, Doljani, these names, these villages, I didn't know anything about them, I didn't know who the inhabitants were. And in talking to the duty operative down there, I asked him about the buses, considering that he knew something about these buses, that he knew everything about the buses. He says, Who, what, where, when, how? And then I said, Well, they're supposed to drive somebody from Sovici and Doljani. Who those people are, probably the greens, because I knew that Sovici were an exit to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this document you wrote could be incriminatory: "Have five buses come to Sovici or Doljani to evacuate the population," in brackets "green," "towards Jablanica. If they have, where did they come from." This is what you wrote. And when reading it, it seems that you sending five buses to evacuate the civilians, which is fine, but you seem to wonder what on earth these people are doing there. If they are there, where are they coming from? So one could think that according to you, there were no longer any civilians there, and then Halilovic is suddenly telling you, But there are Muslims in Sovici and Doljani, and you seem surprised. And so you're asking the question, Well, if they're there, where did they come from? What do you have to say on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's wrong. From the film -- well, the previous day it was said that there were a thousand dead over there, or incarcerated, or -- well, Arif Pasalic said, Doljani, Sovici, the day before, and now this name is a name I hear for the first time, this place name. I didn't go to Sovici and Doljani, so I don't know what they were dealing with there, Sefer and Petkovic. What I do know is they said, Check and see whether the buses have arrived in Doljani. And so I didn't find my way very well there, and then I talked to the duty officer in the military district and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish my question. This is my interpretation of this document, and you can agree with it or not. I might be wrong, of course. A military action is underway in Sovici and Doljani. Whether either by the HVO or the BH Army, I'm not going into details to know exactly who did what, but there are combats. Fighting is going on between soldiers. It seems that whenever there is fighting, the civilian population might be there, but sometimes is no longer there. At the HVO level, you know that there is fighting, and you believe that the civilians are all gone. But then suddenly Halilovic is telling Petkovic, during this meeting, that there are civilians in the area. Now, of course, you do not know in neither Sovici nor Doljani, and you do what is needed to send the buses, which is a humanitarian gesture that no one could blame you for. But at the same time, you seem to be very surprised to suddenly find out that there are civilians, and in this question [as interpreted] you actually put the question about the civilians. That's what I'm trying to understand, so please answer honestly. There's no need to beat around the bush.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that in Sovici and Doljani, what I understood was that there was a population there, and later on, with the actors of the conflict, I gain a picture of what was happening over there. And when I was asked whether the buses had left, I didn't know. I talked to Piske, Cibo, Polo, Zuka, Nihad, Cibo, so that I could gain an impression about Sovici and Doljani to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, it's noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm trying to make myself understood. The President has put it to you that this was a fine humanitarian gesture. That is quite possible. I think it is a one-sided view. Maybe it's right. But one could also say that this is a piece of ethnic cleansing, because you only take away the greens. You know nothing about the places, you say. How do you know that there's only greens there and that there are no Croats that need protection? This is what I find a bit strange. I wonder whether you have an explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I'm surprised that various insinuations are now being made about all this. The whole problem of Doljani and Sovici I see as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please don't say that you're surprised. Judges have to check all the different assumptions, those who are in favour of a case and those who go against a case also. That's the role they're supposed to play. A Judge is not supposed to take the written word at face value. It tries to understand and to check the different assumptions. And my colleague, my fellow Judge, is trying to check a hypothesis. It's not an insinuation. He's trying to verify a situation, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday I transferred Muslim refugees from Vasic when the Serbs had expelled them, and then I said, Send ambulances. Who's being driven? The greens are. So this is certainly the Muslim population, and it's certain that there were Muslim inhabitants there. Now, why they needed the buses, they need it for Jablanica. If they were going to Jablanica, then it was quite certain that they were greens. So I asked whether the buses had been sent and had arrived to transport the greens to Jablanica. There were no blues going to Jablanica, no way. So it was quite clear to me that it was the greens that were going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it's time for the break, so we shall break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I continue, I'd like to make a request, if I may. We're dealing with Sovici and Doljani, and on the first document that I showed, with respect to your questions we came to something that was supposed to be my conclusion with the witness; that is to say, how and why the HVO secured the buses, whether it was just responding to a request from the BH Army or, alternatively, was it assistance to the HVO so that Sefer Halilovic could cleanse Sovici and Doljani, or, as a third possibility, that the HVO independently ethnically cleansed Sovici and Doljani. I would like to assure you that I intend to discuss this matter with the witness, but could you allow me to conduct my examination-in-chief as I had planned to do? And when I complete my examination, if I don't succeed in receiving an answer or fail to raise those very important questions, then you can, of course, step in.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, one more question on the document that I assume is still on our screens, your request about the buses or query about the buses. The last sentence: "If they have, where do they come from?" Does that sentence relate to the buses who were supposed to come to Sovici and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is 4D447, and it's a document from the BH Army, a report dated the 4th of May. And roughly in the middle of that document, it says that: "For tomorrow, we have agreed the unconditional evacuation of the civilian population from Doljani and Sovici." My question to you, General, is this: In your opinion and to the best of your knowledge at the time, was it the evacuation of the civilian population which the HVO -- and the HVO laid down no conditions; is that what it's about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The witness said a few moments ago, under oath, that he knew nothing about what happened in Sovici/Doljani, so I don't understand how he can answer these questions. He said earlier this afternoon, on page 24 of the transcript: "I didn't go to Sovici and Doljani, so I don't know what they were dealing with there." He's never been there, doesn't know anything about it, I have no idea how these questions can be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mr. Scott, at face value you are no doubt right, but the problem regarding this document is that the document shows that there was a meeting, and apparently the witness attended the meeting. So even though he doesn't know those two villages, it may be that he knew or heard from Mr. Halilovic that the civilian population had to be evacuated; hence the document, the BH Army document. But you're right, he did say that he did not know what happened in those villages. But we're going to see more clearly through Ms. Alaburic's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, further on that, Your Honour, just for one more moment, Your Honour, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I also just remind -- I'll remind the Chamber of the Judges, your questions, before the break and questions as to why he -- how he didn't know that there were civilians in the area and how -- what he had thought was going on. And again, Your Honour, I take it when you take the answers to Your Honours' questions, the President's questions, and Judge Trechsel's questions before the break, and his testimony that he didn't know what was happening there, had never been there, didn't know what they were dealing with, but again he has no basis to answer these questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me explain. I'm not asking the witness about the events in Sovici and Doljani now, in the sense of war activities. I'm asking the witness about the evacuation of the civilian population from Doljani and Sovici, and I'd like to remind you of two statements made by the witness. First of all, he said, when first asked, that he knew nothing about it, and he didn't even know where Sovici and Doljani were located, but then he went on to say that he talked about it to Arif Pasalic, and then mentions Zuka, and Cibo, and polo, and all the rest of them. So what the witness learnt in talking to these people, we'll hear about that later on. But now what I'm asking -- I'm asking this witness -- well, if the witness knows nothing about the topic of the evacuation and the conditions of the HVO, the witness will be able to say so. So there's no fear that the witness won't answer in the manner in which he thinks best, under oath or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, my question to you, General: To the best of your knowledge, did the HVO place any conditions for the civilian population to be evacuated from Sovici and Doljani, lay any conditions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object to the use of the term "evacuation." It's an argumentative term. The term -- she can talk about transportation, the people were transported. Of course, in the Tuta Stela case, both the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber rejected any notion that this was an evacuation, clearly concluded that. That's an adjudicated fact found in this case. It was not an evacuation, could not have been an evacuation. And if counsel wants to pursue the matter further, she should, please, use a neutral term and not "evacuation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, regarding your objections, let me read out what Judge Robinson said in the Kordic case, that you know perfectly well. On page 17140, this is what Judge Robinson said: "Mr. Sayers, the less objections you raise, the faster we will move on. I'm going to listen to you. However, I wish to remind you that you were interrupted only very rarely during cross-examination conducted by you, and remember to behave in a similar fashion." So Judge Robinson, who's now the President of the Tribunal, who's a very experienced man, who is of a common-law tradition, remembers and reminds that the lawyer isn't supposed to raise objections for objection's sake; it's a waste of time. We understood your first objection. Ms. Alaburic was made aware of the problem, which she understood, and no doubt she's going to put questions in order to highlight what the witness knew or did not know. And thereafter, the Judges will rule. Please continue, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me just a sentence to respond to my learned friend Scott concerning adjudicated facts from the Tuta Stela case. From his remark, I would conclude that Mr. Scott is not familiar with the fact that adjudicated facts can be challenged in this proceedings. I would like to say that I'm well familiar with adjudicated facts from the Tuta Stela case, and this is because -- exactly why I'm trying to challenge them using BiH Army documents and not HVO documents, because I want for the facts to be determined accurately and comprehensively. So my question to the witness, the witness uses the term "evacuation" because this term is used by the BiH Army, 44th Mountain Brigade Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My question to you is: From your knowledge of that day, did HVO impose any conditions on the evacuation of the civilian population from Sovici and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no conditions imposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, at that point in time did you know that the Croatian population from that part of the Jablanica municipality had been evacuated in the direction of Posusje?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Please, Witness, after first learning about Sovici and Doljani, did you try to find out from anybody what had happened, really, in those villages in the municipality of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this emerged as the main problem after the first meeting, I tried to quiz the immediate actors who were at that meeting, and subsequently I tried to find out what had happened. The commander of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade was among them. I believe the family name was Sagolj, aka Piske, and the battalion commander within that brigade, in charge of Sovici and Doljani, I remembered him as "Marco Polo," but his name was Stipo or Cipe, on the one hand. And on the other hand, I spoke to Zuka, Nihad, and Cibo about the same thing, and I tried to compose a picture of those events in my mind of those events in that cluster of villages in that valley, bearing in mind my experiences of events in other areas, because I did not fall from Mars there. So my knowledge about Sovici and Doljani in those days was complete for my purposes, in my capacity as a member of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a series of questions, and depending on your answers, you should tell us whether you learned that from Muslims or Croats. In Sovici and Doljani, were there any murdered civilians?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sovici and Doljani, there were no civilians killed, and there was no destruction, as was customary in other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, did you receive any information to the effect that in Sovici and Doljani, any Muslim woman had been raped?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am surprised by this question, but this never cropped up in any negotiations as an issue. So my answer is, No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, you say that you have not been in Sovici and Doljani. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, personally, was not there. I visited other axes, Kostajnica and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So it is simply hearsay when you affirm today that there are no destructions there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was second-hand information, but from both sides to the conflict. I did not rely upon only information from one side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us, what did you hear? What was the main problem at Sovici and Doljani? What crime did happen there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Perhaps he could tell us the source of this information, too, so we could have a chance to check on it, rather than general, vague allegations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to remind everybody that the witness precisely said who he spoke to on the Croatian side and on the Muslim side. So, please, my learned friend Scott should peruse the transcript and then clarify the matter in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I want to know who said what. I don't want just general things floating around about he talked to three or four nameless people or people we don't know who they are, and then just said, Someone told me that. I want to know who told him which specific things so that, if necessary, I can send investigators into the field to contact those people and see if it's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in order not to waste any time, can you tell us who told you what, specifically? Or it may be that you can't remember, which is perfectly comprehensible. But if you do remember, who told you what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Piske, the brigade commander - I believe his family name was Sagolj - told me that two brigades attacked his brigade from the north and the east, the Konjic Brigade and the Neretvica Brigade respectively, and that from behind he was attacked by the Jablanica Brigade, brigades of the Territorial Defence of the Army of BiH, in the direction of Kostajnica and Boksevica. In the latter case, the case of the Jablanica Brigade of the Territorial Defence, at one point they cut off the communication or captured the saddle named "Sovicka Vrata," which is the part or section on the salvation road, as we called it. It is a watershed between the Rama Valley and the Listica Valley or the Blidnje lake, and by doing so they cut off and encircled his battalion. And heading that battalion was Stjepan Tole -- sorry, Stjepan Polo. Well, "Marco Polo" was the way I remembered his name. So this was this battalion encircled, and that battalion belonged to the aforementioned brigade. Then, by an action of the HVO or, if I'm not mistaken, by an action of a battalion, the so-called Convicts Battalion, they resolved the issue of the Sovici gateway or the saddle, and they lifted the encirclement around that battalion, and allegedly everything calmed down. In later combat two or three days subsequently, part of the Convicts Battalion, or elements of that battalion, intervened, or attacked, or defended themselves at a feature where this one Cikota was killed, and he was one of the commanders or heroes from the ranks of that unit. When they buried Cikota, they came to that village and raised hell, in terms of harassing the population, torching the houses, and Polo stood up to them, and he told me that he even reported that to the Main Staff. I tried to verify those facts from Zuka and Nihad who are, on the other side, were in charge of that situation. Of course, they interpret the events differently, and Zuka told me, What do you mean, Sovici gateway? It's impossible for there not to have been harassment, and that they had not captured the Sovici gateway, and that they had not been there, and that everything was invented by Piske and Polo. If I may continue. So when they buried that individual Cikota, they came there, they raised hell, but there were no casualties, reportedly. There were some houses torched, and the population was afraid, and the population was then supposed to be sent to Jablanica, but was directed instead towards Prozor and Gornji Vakuf. And from Arif Pasalic, the subsequent day he sought from me oil or fuel and buses to bus people from Gornji Vakuf to Jablanica, so I found out then that they had not gone to Jablanica, but to Gornji Vakuf. I also learned later on why they had not been taken to Jablanica; because of the marble blocks on the road disrupting traffic. This is what I learned from Piske and Polo and, on the other hand, from Zuka and Nihad.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to show you a statement of a witness in this courtroom. I tried to find out whether it was a protected witness. I hope I'm not going to make a mistake. His name is Nihad Kovac. He was a witness of Sovici and Doljani. 10307 is the page of the transcript, and we have his words. In a statement he prepared for the Prosecution, and during examination by the Prosecutor, he said that the houses in Sovici and Doljani were torched on the 18th, maybe later, maybe after the 20th. And during my cross-examination, I asked him to focus and try to tell us precisely whether the houses had been torched on the 18th or on the 21st, because it was extremely important for us in this case. And Nihad Kovac said that he thought that the houses were torched on the 21st, and that was the day after the burial of Cikota, one of the commanders in the Convicts Battalion. Tell us, what you heard from Nihad Kovac, is that the same what you learned with the interlocutors that you named?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, after the intervention in the area of the Sovici gateway and control of the overall territory, everything calmed down. What I do know, that the population was harassed and the houses were torched later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine, General. Let's take a look at the next document, P2195. It is an information produced by the BiH Army, signed by Enver Zejnilagic, and it discusses the Halilovic-Petkovic agreement, but also says that the HVO, at their own initiative, sent the civilians to Gornji Vakuf. You, Witness, said that you heard about the civilians from Sovici/Doljani being directed towards Gornji Vakuf. Does this document correspond to your knowledge of the matter of the time?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were supposed to go to Jablanica initially, but I learned that they went to Gornji Vakuf because of the road being blocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at the next document, 4D1079, 4D1079. The second page, under item 1 of this document, a commission comprised of two representatives of the Croatian side say: "One of the commissions visited areas of Sovici, Doljani, and Slatina in the presence of General Petkovic and Halilovic. Everything asked was realised." Please tell us, General, did the Muslim side require the Croatian side of the HVO to get the buses for the transport of the Sovici and Doljani civilians?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this whole case, there's no doubt about it, because Arif subsequently sought that I provide the fuel for the buses to transport them back, which means that the Muslim side required the transport of those civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next document, 4D430. This is another BiH Army document. In the lower part of the document, towards the end, dated on the 17th of April, 1993, so this was way before this evacuation, it is stated: "The Gornji Vakuf-Prozor-Jablanica road is prepared for completion, and in a section of the road in the village of Gornja Slatina there are obstructions made of granite blocks which cannot be moved, so passage is possible only by small passenger vehicles in emergency cases." And there is another document discussing the same topic, the other being P1911. I'm going to ask you questions about both. And this is a document by the European Union Monitoring Mission or European Community Monitoring Mission. Item 5(b), it is stated that on the approach-way from Prozor to Jablanica by Slatina, there is a strong fortified position where passage of vehicles is barred by large granite blocks. General, please tell us whether these reports correspond to your knowledge about the obstructions on the road towards Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: From these documents, from the descriptions, I can say that this is the obstruction that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P2825.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Again, Witness, I would like to know: Did you actually see the blocks or is this also hearsay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see those blocks because I did not go in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, please tell us -- you've already told us that are not an immediate eye-witness in that area, but could you tell us whether you had any cause to doubt BiH Army officers and European Monitoring Mission members, or other people you spoke to would lie about obstructions on that road, barring large vehicles from passing the place?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, there is a quarry very close by, and there are huge blocks, five- ten-ton blocks. There's plenty of that. I don't know what was the size of those blocks on the road, but there's no doubt and there's no cause for them to lie. First of all, this is not an HVO source, and, on the other hand, these are professionals.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's take a look at P2825. This is an SIS Information from the North-West Herzegovina Operations Zone which states that in the period from the 10th to the 15th of June, 1993, from Gornji Vakuf via Dobrosine and Privor and further down the road towards Jablanica, eight buses carrying refugees passed. Those refugees come from Doljani and Sovici. They were transferred to Gornji Vakuf, and now they're being transferred to Jablanica. General, please tell us, did you have knowledge that ultimately civilians of Muslim ethnicity were transferred to Jablanica, as had been promised to them by Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any knowledge about that. And on the 18th of June, at that period, I was in Central Bosnia. I could have learnt about it, but not in any such detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When Arif Pasalic asked you to secure fuel, petrol, and the buses for the inhabitants of Sovici and Doljani to be transferred from Gornji Vakuf to Jablanica, did you undertake anything in respect of that request, demand?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I insisted with the Main Staff. I prevailed upon them to see that it was carried out. Now, why they didn't go to Jablanica, I don't know, and all these problems about the check-points along the way and so on. But you're asking me about the document dated the 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say when.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when they were sent back, the people from Gornji Vakuf, to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, on the basis of all the knowledge you have about the events --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before you continue on, if counsel could assist us with clarifying the question on page 40, line 4: "When Arif Pasalic asked you to secure fuel, petrol, and the buses for the inhabitants of Sovici and Doljani to be transferred from Gornji Vakuf to Jablanica," if my memory is mistaken, I apologise, but the only testimony I recall so far is the arrangement of buses to take people from Sovici to somewhere else, and it turned out that the allegation is instead of going to Jablanica it went to Gornji Vakuf, and I don't recall any evidence about there being a second arrangement for buses to go -- for Mr. Pasalic to go from Gornji Vakuf to Jablanica. And if I'm mistaken, if that can be indicated, I'll appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can tell my learned friend Mr. Scott that he's wrong, because the witness said quite clearly that from Arif Pasalic he learned that the civilians had been transferred to Gornji Vakuf and not to Jablanica. But anyway, Witness, you can tell us that yourself, but I don't want this to be deducted from my own time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, when and how did you learn that the civilians had gone to Gornji Vakuf and what did you talk about to Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already the next day, I think it was the 6th, Arif Pasalic was very angry and asked why the civilians had gone to Gornji Vakuf, and he said that I should secure the fuel needed - I didn't have any fuels - and get the buses to return these civilians to Jablanica. So that was his ultimatum. He wanted the population to be returned to Jablanica. And that's when I learnt that this transport had been carried out, as I asked about the buses, and it wasn't to Jablanica but to Gornji Vakuf, and now what had to be organised was the return of these people to Jablanica. And I -- well, with all the other problems that I had to solve, Pasalic and I and all those meetings that we had and so on, I don't know exactly when they were returned. And from this document, the 6th, I see that I wasn't there already at that time, but I don't know what the exact date was and whether they were returned at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, this request from Arif Pasalic, did you convey it to the Main Staff for them to find buses and so that the inhabitants of Sovici and Doljani could be transported from Gornji Vakuf to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, you get up in the morning at 5.00 or 6.00 a.m., you get into an IPS, and you go to Jablanica, or Konjic, or wherever else. You spend the whole day there. When you come back in the evening, you take out your little notebook to see what you need to do, and I'm sure that I conveyed this request for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I? Excuse me. Witness, maybe I have missed something and ought to know; then, please, I apologise. I would like to know who actually put those granite blocks on the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The TO, or, rather, the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, that is, because given the place that it was at, it must have been the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I find it difficult to understand, having some familiarity with what the military can do, why they were not blown up. Blocks can be blown up. You have lots of explosives. You drill a hole, you put in an explosive, you close it, and, boom, the block is manageable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where would we get explosives from, Your Honour Judge Trechsel? Where would we get the explosives from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I did not ask a question of you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, please let the witness answer. He has the same competence as you, and he can answer this technical question put to him by a Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel said that it's easy in the army, it's easy to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He says it's easy; you just get some explosives, warehouses are full of explosives, and then you just blow it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that the blocks were heavy, they were large blocks. I don't know how they managed to put them there in the first place, but probably they rolled them there. But to remove them would be a greater problem. I don't know how Petkovic and Sefer managed to pass through at all. Perhaps smaller vehicles were able to pass through, but buses or large trucks with trailers, they wouldn't be able to pass. But to remove this obstacle was a very difficult thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will soon have the opportunity to ask General Petkovic about these granite blocks as well, but let's return to Arif Pasalic now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Anyway, you were with him for quite a long time during those days; isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you, at some time in that first half of May 1993, go back to the Mostar area with Arif Pasalic from this area of Jablanica and Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least two or three times together in an APC.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you were together in one APC, were you?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in your return on the 8th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, 1993, we were in Jablanica, and in Konjic, for that matter, and then we stayed for quite some time, and it was already getting dark when we left Jablanica with these APCs. Carlos was the commander, and the journey -- well, you couldn't see anything through those slits on the APC. We arrived -- I was already sleeping, but we reached Dracevo, and Dracevo is south of Capljina, near Metkovici. It was the headquarters or base of the battalion and its unit. And suddenly we stepped down from the APC. There was some white containers. And they asked us whether we were going to stay together or whether we would continue on separately. But Arif Pasalic and I, for four days, were stopped by UNPROFOR. There were guards. Just let me paint this picture. If I wanted to go to the toilet, for example, I'd open the door and I'd have a rifle cocked at me. I went to search for the toilet. He said, Wait. Ten minutes later, a jeep turned up with a driver and two soldiers at the back. I got into the jeep. They drove me 50 metres off to the toilet, and I returned. So we were guarded in this way. So that four days later, Sefer and Petkovic arrived, and the two of us went to Medjugorje, for direct negotiations there that were being held in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the Prosecutor claimed in these proceedings that the HVO prevented the exit of Sefer Halilovic on that day, the 8th or 9th of May, 1993, in Mostar because -- "Pasalic," I meant to say. The departure of Arif Pasalic, I meant to say, Arif Pasalic's departure during those days in the Mostar area. And the reason they gave was that the HVO was preparing an attack against the BH Army in Mostar, that that was the reason, and that this conduct towards Arif Pasalic, he wanted to leave the BH Army without the number-one man. So can you now, General, comment on this assertion made? Was that the truth of it or not?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The route we followed passes mostly through an area controlled by the BH Army, and I don't know how the HVO could prevent Arif Pasalic from leaving the APC.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Your Honours, that completes the topic of Sovici and Doljani, if anybody has some questions to ask on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I listened very carefully to the questions put to you by Ms. Alaburic. When she asked all these questions on May 8th, I listened even more closely. If I understand you correctly, on May 8, 1993, you are with Arif Pasalic, and you are in an armoured vehicle, the both of you, plus Carlos and a fourth person, because I believe that you said there were four of you in the APC. You said, I slept, and then we arrived, and we were guarded for four days. So that means 8 May plus four days, that's May 12. On May 9, an event occurred in Mostar, and the Trial Chamber will have to determine who actually attacked, whether it was the BH Army or the HVO. Let's assume that the BH Army attacked. The commander of the 4th Corps is Mr. Arif Pasalic, but he's with you on May 9. And according to what you say, it seems that you were more or less prisoner, a prisoner of the international forces. If you had to go to the toilet, you had to have an escort. Now, here are my questions: First, why did the international forces keep you for four days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because later on I learnt -- or, rather, on the second and third day, judging by the artillery fire, I realised that there was a conflict going on, and probably during that conflict they kept us in Mostar. Two or three days later, I learned about this. Or they couldn't, perhaps, transfer us elsewhere, so I was held there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are telling us is very new. We never heard of this. So you were arrested, but you were not the only one; Pasalic also was under arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Pasalic too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Militarily-wise, if the BH Army attacks the HVO, does this mean that his commander, Mr. Pasalic, needs to be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole day of the 8th, and on the 6th and 7th, he was attending negotiations, trying to solve the problem in Konjic and Jablanica. So the whole day on the 8th, as well, he was in Konjic and Jablanica. We set out in the evening, when it grew dark. Now, where he should have been, in my view, he should have been where he was, since we were solving -- trying to resolve this problem of the conflict, and we'd been doing that for the past fortnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During four days you spent with him, was it possible for you to communicate or to contact your own soldiers or your own line of command? What about him; was he able to call Halilovic or not? Were you really under arrest, in custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't give us any transistors, or radios, or newspapers or any information whatsoever for the first three days. It was only on the fourth day that the commander organised a lunch with us, and these two men came at that moment and took us to Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
