utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard a whole series -- a whole battalion of people who came to testify, and if I had known this, I would have put this question to them. I would have asked them why they kept a high military representative of the HVO, i.e., you, and Mr. Pasalic in custody for four days. I would have been very interested in their answer. Unfortunately, I'm just discovering this after the fact. Let's go back to Sovici and Doljani. Ms. Alaburic did not really spend a lot of time on these issues. I believe that she's waiting for Mr. Petkovic to testify to go into details. But you briefly skimmed on a number of things, and they drew my attention. Cikota was killed, and then he's buried. Unless I'm wrong, I believe that when General Praljak was testifying, he said he went to his burial and then he left. Now, you are saying that after the burial, the soldiers of the Convicts Battalion went over there and abused the local population. You said this, and no one reacted. But according to what you know, can you confirm that the events which occurred in Sovici and Doljani were carried out by soldiers of the Convicts Battalion who went there after Cikota's burial, maybe to commit this abuse, maybe for retaliation, or I don't know for what reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Praljak, I don't know about that. I don't know that he was attending a burial funeral. But from talking to Marko Polo, or Stipo Polo, rather, it was clear that they went to the village after the funeral and all hell broke loose there - that's what I realised after the burial - out of hatred or retaliation or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Kordic case, and I could show you that questions and answers were asked publicly and this is public knowledge, out of memory -- I don't have the page with me, but out of memory, I think you said that according to you, there were some rogue units. Now, can you tell us whether the Convicts Battalion was actually controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were units at both sides which were and were not under control. They were because they're part of the composition of the HVO, when they had to receive something from the HVO. But when they wanted to do something or not to do something, to go to the defence line, then they were not under control. There were groups of people or units whose use could be questionable in comparison with other units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not really answering the question. I would like to know whether the Convicts Battalion was controlled by the HVO. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about the group Vitezovi or Knights in Vitez. I don't know about the Convicts Battalion. Most probably, it wasn't. I don't know. I cannot confirm either way because I was not in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know. Very well. But you added that the Vitezovi were rogue, were a rogue unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could not command them. I could not instruct them to go to the defence line, like I could in the case of other units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because from the very beginning they were an HOS unit which was not part of the HVO, but later on it was part of the HVO. It was headed by Darko Kraljevic, who was as he was. He, in the darkest hours for Vitez, he managed to get a special status for him and his unit to hold as much defence line as he wanted, and he was different from the other units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, I believe you have 35 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I almost thought there was 37, not 35. Well, it was a mistake in translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let's discuss joint command and joint commission. First, let's take a look at 1467. Your Honours, that would be in the first binder. It could be the last or the penultimate block of issues. General, please look at the screen so that we don't waste time looking for the documents. I'm going to ask you simple questions. So it would be P1467. It is an order by Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic, dated 11th of February, 1993, stating that the commanders of the 3rd Corps of the army and the HVO operations zone establish a joint co-ordinations team comprised of three members per side, and then there is a list of definitions of that team's tasks. General, you can see the first page of this document. Tell us, did you know that in mid-February a co-ordinations team was established, headed by Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next document, 4D1205. General, I'm shifting my sequence of documents. Please take a look at the screen. Sir, this is a set of documents co-signed by Blaskic and Hadzihasanovic. Each of them pertains to a different topic. I'm going to list all of them, and finally I'm going to ask you, General, whether you had any knowledge of those orders and whether they had been carried out. The first of all is to remove all roadblocks and obstacles from all communications. The second is at the level of all municipalities, commissions should be established to work towards calming down the situation. The third was to fill with earth all trenches and bunkers, and after the withdrawal of units from the contact line, that all places to be visited and toured. Fourth, that all transports which had been stopped should be let through to get to their destinations. Fifth, to form check-points to control the goods, to be manned by the representatives of the two armies, together with civilian representatives. The sixth, to release all prisoners unconditionally, prisoners and detained persons. The seventh, to secure the conditions for the return of those who are refugees. The next is to urgently withdraw units from the contact line. So, General, these orders are dated the 13th of February, 1993. Did you know that Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic had issued orders of this kind?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a practice throughout that time, first conflict and then trying to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm skipping four documents, if you are trying to follow me in your binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a follow-up question. Earlier on, we saw a document signed by the 3rd Corps commander. That was speaking about the roadblocks, or the marble blocks, rather, on the road, and this is confirmed in the document by Hadzihasanovic. So what you observed is supported by this document. But this makes me revisit the question put by my fellow Judge, without an answer. You said, Well, if there are blocks on the road, you can push them aside. If they're so big that you can't push them aside, can't you use explosives to destroy them, by digging a hole into them and putting dynamite to blow them up? And if you don't have the equipment, can't you turn to the Logistics Section in your brigade, or in the operative zone, or still in the headquarters, for them to provide you with the explosives in order to blow up the blocks that prevent traffic? That is an everyday occurrence, isn't it? When I was in Switzerland, I saw blocks that had fallen on the road, and you have some people in charge of maintaining the roads that do that every day. Were you that deprived? Because that seems to be what General Praljak says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An obstacle may be removed in a certain way, using a certain method, if there is the will to remove it. If there's the will to remove it, there will be a way to do it, if there's time; maybe a big vehicle to drag it away, or by explosives, depending on the type of the obstacle. If there is a will to remove it, it can be removed using an appropriate method.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So when there's a will, there's a way. But obviously there was no will here; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us who removes obstacles in which territory? Would the HVO remove obstacles in the area controlled by the Croats or would they go into the Muslim-controlled territory to remove obstacles?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Territorial Defence is removing an HVO obstacle, then conflict ensues, combat ensues, and vice versa. If there is an obstacle introduced by the TO or the Army of BiH, then they have to remove it, otherwise there is conflict, conflagration.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly? Each side should remove obstacles in their territory if they want to do so?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if in Ahmici the obstacle is there, then the TO or the BiH Army has to remove it. Otherwise, the HVO must use armed force to do it, or conversely in Jablanica, but in the period of agreements or talks, so conflicts are out of the question. Now, it only boils down to the method to remove the obstacle in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine, General. Let's discuss joint command. Let's take a look at 4D455. The document will be shown on your screen. And before it appears on the screen, I will describe it. It is a decision on the appointment of members of the Joint Command of the HVO and the ABiH, the nomination of the Croatian representatives to that body, signed by the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. It is dated the 26th of April, 1993, and here, General, we can see that on behalf of the Croats, you, Mario Andric and Zuka Totic are nominated into that Joint Command. Please tell us, General, were you really nominated into the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Totic was nominated or was supposed to be appointed at my insistence to free him from captivity, because the Mujahedin had him captured, and so I wanted to release him by him being nominated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. And from this document on nomination, it follows that joint commands have been established at the levels of operations zones and corps levels. Was this so, General?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can list you the names of the people at least in the military district or the corps, where their seats were, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to do so had we had time, but let's look at the next document, P2155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, General. You said so in the Kordic case, when you testified about Totic, you said that he had been appointed because he had been detained and that was a way of releasing -- or having him released. Now, we have here an appointment. It is dated the 26th of April. General Petkovic is the one who is appointing him and signed the text, but he signed on a proposal coming from you or was it his own idea to appoint Totic to the Joint Command to exert pressure on the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order dated 26th was the culmination of the preceding activities concerning the nomination and appointment. Previously, I had been quizzed whether I would concede to go to the Joint Command, and I acceded to that suggestion. And so in our talks, I don't know whether Blaskic or Petkovic, because we'd met this day, I insisted for Totic to be released. He was from my tactical group, a commander in Zenica. This is what I had insisted on, and Petkovic must have acceded to that because eventually he signed that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take the next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P2155 is going to appear on your screen? It is an order co-signed by Petkovic and Halilovic, dated the 30th April 1993, implementation of joint commands at the level of operative zones or corps, and it is stated that that command will be comprised of: Hadzihasanovic, Blaskic, and their deputies, et cetera. General, did you know that Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic would lead the Joint Command at operation zone or corps level.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did leave, but there were also Nakic. From the corps of the operations zone, we had Nakic nominated to the Joint Command, and Juric, but I'm not sure about the latter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 4D594.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, this is one of the very few documents in which we can find "ABiH" and "HVO." Look at the letterhead of the document. We can see "Joint Command of the BH Army and HVO." Under that, there is the reference number. It's "Broj" in your language, isn't it, "1-2"? Can you confirm that this is one of the first documents co-signed by General Petkovic and General Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the position of the Joint Command, yes, but they signed some other documents. But, yes, with respect to the Joint Command, this concerns Zenica. I wasn't in Zenica. I was shown the apartment where I was supposed to be. And these are one of the first documents of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may not have an answer to this. You never know. But, you know, Judges are curious by nature, they put questions, and then sometimes the answer crops up. How is it that in this official document - it was signed by two high-ranking officers - how is it that there's no letterhead saying "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer this question, whether there's no reference of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember the question, I'll put it in due time to General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's see who was in the command at the level of the corps of the operative zone. And for that, let's look at 4D594.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is an order from Tihomir Blaskic, dated the 1st of May, 1993, on the establishment of a joint command of the three armies at the level of the operative zone -- or, rather, corps, and mention is made here of the gentlemen, two of whom you mentioned yourself; is that right, General.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I forget to mention Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That command worked at the level of the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Here's another document on that same topic, P2726, 2726. It's an agreement signed in Kiseljak on the 10th of June, 1993, signed by Petkovic and Rasim Delic. And in item 2, General, it says here -- or, rather, your name is mentioned here. Tell us, please, were you at that meeting that resulted in this agreement?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petkovic and I came from the Prozor area. We went to Kiseljak. And on the 9th, we were supposed to meet with Sefer to discuss the various activities; I mean, Sefer and others. However, Siber and Karisik came to negotiate, because Petkovic didn't want to talk to a level which was not suitable. So I talked to them on the first day. Then Delic arrived on the second day, and the explanation was that there'd been a replacement in the BH Army. Instead of Sefer Delic [as interpreted], that the number-one man came and these were talks and negotiations. However, after all these talks and negotiations, later on I felt in the field, when I was in the field, well, the worst period in the war started from that point onwards, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said "Sefer Delic." Who was appointed to the function?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Delic, Rasim. Rasim Delic, instead of Sefer Halilovic, is what I meant. I knew many of these people personally, I knew theirs names, their nicknames, so just ask me if you need explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just, tell me in a word. Well, you said that you knew Rasim Delic from before. What was your opinion of him, as a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I knew Delic from 1967. When he was a cadet, I was a year older. I knew him through his years of service. He replaced me as Chief of Staff when I went to Derventa. Anyway, as far as I know, he's one of the most capable officers that they had, and it seemed logical to me that this replacement should have taken place, Sefer and Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let's go back to our Central Bosnia of April 1993. Your Honours, that's the subject that was dealt with in the first part of the binder, so before the Joint Command issue. I'm going to skip over two documents and move on to 4D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, regarding the last document that was signed in Kiseljak, were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, both days, both days at the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I noted that this document, too, was co-signed by Mr. Jean-Pierre Thebault and by Brigadier Hayes. Do you remember these two internationals being present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were present, but I knew Thebault better because he was in Central Bosnia more than this other one, Hayes. Morillon was before that, and then Hayes came afterwards. But, yes, I did know them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did these two individuals co-sign this document? What did their signature mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What it signified was this: As witnesses, they confirmed it, they strengthened the agreement. Their signatures, first and foremost, meant that they were there when the agreement was reached, and, secondly, that the international community stood behind it, supported it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A bit of a mystery. This is a document in B/C/S. I suppose that Mr. Thebault and Mr. Hayes did not speak your language; did they? So how did it take place? Was it translated to them, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They always had translators -- interpreters going with them, and the document was harmonised. They knew what was written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since I intend to discuss Central Bosnia as another area with this witness, perhaps we could take a break now, and then I could go into that matter without interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we have half an hour left, roughly, so let's try and deal with Central Bosnia for a bit, and let's start off with April 1993. The first document that I'd like us to discuss is 4D597, and along with that document we have prepared a map. Their Honours have the map. May we provide the witness with it, and place it on the ELMO, please. In the meantime, let me say that the document that we have before us now is a preparatory combat order from Tihomir Blaskic of the 15th of April, 1993. Otherwise, it's an exhibit in the Blaskic trial. And we would like to focus on item 2 of that combat order, where Tihomir Blaskic assesses the axis of attack by the BH Army. I hope this time isn't being deducted from my overall time. Your Honour, I don't think it's fair, really, to deduct time that is needed for documents to be located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you think it would be fair to change the rules at this point in the proceedings? I don't think so. I'm sorry. It was fair and unfair to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, when you see that the witness finds it hard to locate a document, which is easy to understand, you can tell the usher during the break that you're going to have questions on specific documents, and the usher can find the documents in question and will show them to the witness. This way, you won't waste any time; on the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did provide the usher, during the break, with this map that I intended to have placed on the ELMO, so we're going to work with that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, during the proofing session for your testimony, we prepared this map. You drew the line there, and we coloured it in blue. On both sides of the blue is green. And now let's see what General Blaskic says about the possible axes of attack by the BH Army. He says that the BH Army most probably could take control of Kuber and separate it from Vitez, and that is something that is marked with the number 1. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kuber, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then he goes on to say that the forces of the BH Army want to go across Potrolica [phoen] and Kuber to link up with their forces in Vranjska and Kruscica, and this linking up is the number 2 on the map. So tell us, General, for this link to be effected, they had to go through the territory controlled by the Croatian side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Here on this map, we can see in greater detail that Santici are along the road, and Ahmici is a village a little further from the road. But over the past 20 years, the houses have gone lower down, so the concept of Ahmici is used, the name Ahmici is used to denote all this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So that is the number 3 on the map? That is to say, that in Nadioci and Ahmici, blockades are to be set up; right?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Territorial Defence, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. So that was Tihomir Blaskic's assessment of the situation. And he also goes on to say that he expects an attack on the fire brigade facility and some other localities. Now, tell me, General, mid-April 1993, did the HVO in this area, the area that you were in -- could it have launched an attack against the BH Army, for example, in the direction of Zenica, with the aim of taking control of Zenica, or in a direction which would go towards the south-east, or in any other direction, for that matter? Was the HVO capable of engaging in attack?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say professionally that it was not capable of launching attacks, except diversions, sabotage, smaller operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, would you place your signature on that map with today's date, and then I'd like to ask the usher -- or, rather, I'd like to ask the Court for an IC number for this map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Usher [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC01139. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, now look at your screen, and the documents will come up there, the first of which is 2D288. Yes. 2D288 is an evaluation by the chief of security of the Supreme Command Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina - his name is Fikret Muslimovic - dated the 16th of May, 1993. And he says that it is realistic to expect further tense relations and an all-out military confrontation between the HVO and the BH Army. Now, you knew this man, Fikret Muslimovic. You've already told us that; is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to mention that this is their Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, tell us, General, on the side of the HVO, were there also assessments made that there would be an all-out military confrontation, and was the HVO preparing for such an eventuality, an all-out confrontation?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some documents and preparations for defence against a military confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's look at the next document, which is 4D1198, and this is an order for attack of the 303rd, a famous Zenica Brigade. And in point 4, the commander says what he has decided. And at the very end of item 4, it says: "For further advancement towards the communication line and road running from Busovaca to Vitez." Now, tell us, General, does this order mean that in this area, the Lasva River Valley, units were coming in from Zenica as well?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite definitely. This is an order. Now, when you ask whether there were any HVO preparations, well, you had to prepare for the defence, that's one thing, and this is an order for combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is an order for attack from the BH Army. Let's look at the next document, which is 4D1518, which is a combat report of the 7th Muslim Brigade, in which it says that the unit was sent in the direction of Ilmice [phoen], and I'm going to leave some names out, but the final destination is Ahmici. Tell us, please, General, did you know that in the fighting in and around Ahmici, the 7th Muslim Brigade took part?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is 4D1516. Once again, the 7th Muslim Brigade, and it says that a unit of that brigade carried out its assignment to cleanse Sik [phoen] and Gola Kosa, and that it was ready to take control of the village of Ahmici. Tell us, please, General, during those days was there fighting around Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only around Ahmici, but the broader area around Ahmici. The BH Army took control of the dominant features and elevations in the hinterland at the back of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at document 4D1514. Once again, the 7th Muslim Brigade. The date is the 18th of April, 1993, and I'm interested in item 1.1, where it says that part of the 7th Muslim Brigade was engaged in fighting in the region of Ahmici village jointly with the BH Army and the local population. Tell us, please, General, to the best of your knowledge, the local population who were Muslims, did they help the 7th Muslim Brigade and the BH Army in the fighting against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you say "the local population." It means soldiers who weren't up at the front-line, who were at home, but they were still soldiers in the sense of having weapons and commanders and so on, because the make-up of the unit was of a rural composition. So that's what that means. And when he says, I have cleansed Golo Brdo, that means that there were HVO soldiers up there and he cleansed the area of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at 4D1513 now, the next document. This is also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the lawyer asked a question saying that there was an action by the BH Army and the local population, and you, you say that in your view, the local population, they were actually soldiers. But could there be no other possibility? I'm thinking of civilians who happened to be there, defending as a village defends, taking it in turns with rifles, hunting rifles, or sticks, or God knows what, and who co-operate with the BH Army so that when there is a conflict or a clash, they take part in it, they're involved. Or is that not possible, according to you? Could they only be soldiers on leave, or having a rest, or being at home, who have their own weapons and will then join the BH Army? Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In mixed-population villages which had previously been inhabited by both Muslims and Croats, refugees reached those villages and they were accommodated at those villages. So we have an HVO unit in the village together with a TO unit of that village. Your notion of civilians and whether they could have been in that area, whether there were men who were not soldiers in that area of the Lasva River Valley, there were no men who were not soldiers. They had uniforms and rifles from the age of 18 until a ripe old age. So this formulation, incorporation, and with the support and assistance of the local population, this denotes a platoon, or a company, or even a larger unit being accommodated at that village, and this does not include people with hunting rifles, or pitchforks, or, you know, God knows what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You know, we have seen a lot of documents, and we know that the HVO or the BH Army were initially created from the TO and then from volunteers who came, because there was no mobilisation, as is known, or draft, as is known in some countries. And when you have such a system, it may happen that there are civilians. Take a man who's 22. He doesn't want to be a volunteer, he doesn't want to go and fight. He was not asked to join the TO, or the BH Army, or the HVO. He's just sitting quietly at home, minding his cattle. But he's also a hunter, so he happens to have a hunting rifle. But he's a civilian. He may have a jacket, but he's a civilian. He doesn't have his military booklet. And so suddenly he's been asked to help defend the village, so together with other people he goes to trenches, if there are any, in order to defend and make sure that the village is not attacked, as part of the HVO -- or in the HVO or the BH Army, but he's still not a serviceman. And when there is an attack, he takes his rifle and fires the rifle. Have you come across such situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not exclude the possibility of an exception, but it would be a strict exception. A man of 22 was either away or he was a soldier assigned to a unit. There were such people in Vienna or in The Hague, abroad, but for them to be in that village and not to perform a defence function, that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is another case or situation we've come across. We saw that there were hundreds of thousands of refugees going from towns to villages, et cetera. I have in mind the refugees from Bugojno. And there's all sorts of people among the refugees; civilian populations, soldiers. They're all mingled together. And refugees arrive in a village. Are they civilians, are they military, we don't know. It's total anarchy that prevails. Let us suppose there is an attack against those, quote/unquote "civilians," and if there are civilians among these people, have you come across a situation in which civilians may turn into fighters because they're given rifles, weapons to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are fighters. There is this film "Lost in Translation," and when it comes to terms of "soldier," "fighter," "civilian," we cannot find our bearings, as far as my impression is concerned. Well, there could be exceptions, but I'm talking about the Lasva River Valley. And in Vitez, we forced those who had decisions by the JNA that they were unfit for the army, but we forced them into the trenches because it was a fight for survival. Otherwise, we could not have survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I understand it, in your view there were no civilians, as a matter of fact, apart from women and children. Any man, maybe except very old men, any man could be a soldier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us, could women have been soldiers or have a defence function?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perform a defence function. But when it comes to my part of the world, men are supposed to fight and defend their wars. A certain percentage of women in our units, but these are younger women, without children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let us return to the footage. I remember a woman who was present at that meeting headed by the Spaniard, together with General Petkovic and General Halilovic. In the background, I think I saw a woman standing. Is that right? Or she might have been a long-haired man. I don't know, but I thought it was a woman. Do you remember that there were, in the BH Army or in the HVO, women also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, what awaits us is a more voluminous document from this set. I'm speaking about all the documents until the penultimate in this section. It's 4D1106. General, please try to find that document.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 4D1106. If I may ask Madam Usher to assist. May I refresh your memory, when I ask that this goes for an Enver Hadzihasanovic document, dated October 1993, whereby he reports on the number of men and the equipment in possession of the 3rd Corps. On page 3 of that document, Enver Hadzihasanovic sums up the number of men in his corps. General, please take a look at your screen, and there he says that he had 51.735 soldiers of the 3rd Corps. Please tell us, what is the number of members of the HVO in the Lasva River Valley at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 8.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the ratio of men between the HVO and the BiH Army in the area that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, part of that corps worked in the direction of Kiseljak, but at least two-thirds of the 51.000 were focusing their attention on the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, General, was there any possibility for you to receive assistance by HVO units from any direction?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not even a bird could reach us in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. On the next page, we have a list of weapons available to the 3rd Corps. General, during the proofing session you added up all the howitzers, mortars, and anti-aircraft cannons, anti-aircraft machine-guns, et cetera, so could you please sum it up for us? At that moment, did the HVO possess better equipment or more weapons, and what was the ratio of fire-power between the two sides?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from personal side-arms -- that would be roughly that ratio. As far as heavier weapons are concerned, the truth was not reflected in those tables because tables are used to distribute weapons among corps. Most probably some things were missing; for instance, 150 pieces of heavy artillery, or there were 50 PAT, or anti-aircraft machine-guns, but we would be wasting time if we were adding up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. But what was the ratio of their weapons to the HVO's weapons?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 2:1, even higher than 2:1.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's not just the artillery, it's the question also of ordnance. We were cut off for 10 months, and we could not bring in reinforcements or bring in supplies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mean your problems in ordnance supplies?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 4D1200. This is an UNPROFOR information about the Mujahedin in Central Bosnia. General, do you recall this document? Under item 2, let me jog your memory, it is stated there that the Mujahedin are Muslim fundamentalists, followers of Jihad or holy war, and that the majority of those Mujahedin are foreign nationals, but there are also locals there. And it states that both strands fight within the ranks of the 7th Muslim Brigade, that this is a unit of fundamentalists. It is further on stated that there are other fundamentalist organisations who are not Mujahedin. They group Muslims from abroad and those from Krajina and Banja Luka. They are assault brigades. Under item 7, there is a reference to the 7th Muslim Brigade, which is responsible to the 3rd Corps, but is commanded by the Supreme Command; in other words, Delic, by Delic. So let's not read through this whole document, but please tell us whether what I've just read corresponds to your knowledge about the Mujahedin, or would you have any corrections?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know everything about the Mujahedin. Is this a Hadzihasanovic document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, it's an UNPROFOR document.

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had the same level of knowledge about them as I did. Without denying the Muslims the right to organise themselves as best they could, I must tell you that the arrival of the Mujahedin was an assault not only on the Croats, but on the Muslims as well, in terms of civilisation, in terms of them imposing their world-view, imposing rules that girls should get married at the age of 12 or 13, then introduction of "nikab," which had not been seen for 50, 60 years before that. Then they introduced banners, for instance, a black banner with Arab scripture on it in Zenica. And El Mujahid was one of the bravest units that Alagic commanded, because when we were capturing Kupres jointly in 1994, he told me, I will capture feature 1800. I told him, No, you won't be able to capture that. He said, Well, you know that the only fighters who could take that feature are the Mujahedin. So the elements of the 7th Muslim Brigade, in other words, the Mujahedin who were different from other units, that's something which I felt on my own skin. They assaulted Totic in Zenica. They murdered four of his escort party, and he arrested them. And they released him only when we managed to find eight Mujahedin to exchange them for him. So they had complete disregard for their own personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is going to be your last question. Your time is up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, you can reflect, because I put another question in the meantime. But I put it to you, Ms. Alaburic. On line 9 of page 70, you have said it is an UNPROFOR document. I read, on top, on the right-hand side, within the square "From HQ, BH Command, Kiseljak." How does that go together?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not have the English version of this document, but this is quite clear. UNPROFOR had its main core headquarters for Bosnia-Herzegovina at Kiseljak, and the seat of the UNPROFOR for the whole of the Balkans was in Zagreb. So this is a report from Kiseljak to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And the UNPROFOR in Kiseljak would call itself "HQ, BH Command"? That's what I have in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot tell you how they labelled themselves, but we've seen reams of documents and we know it for a fact that the UNPROFOR's headquarters for Bosnia-Herzegovina was located at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe if I may try an explanation. In the original -- no, in the translation, we have the word "Za BiH," and that might mean "with the BiH." It would then be the UNPROFOR Command located with BiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please, dear colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour, it's clearly stated it's from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic, for interrupting you. I would like to help both of you. It is a UN document, and if you take the left-hand second section, there you see that 2 UNPROFOR liaison headquarter team, headquarters Vicenza, Italy, and then afterwards "in full headquarters, UNPROFOR, Zagreb, headquarters, BritBat." And on the other side, the right side, you will see "from Headquarters BH Command, Kiseljak," which means that the BritBat Command called itself "Headquarters, BH, Kiseljak." So I believe that it is, anyway, a UN -- I mean -- I said "UN," but UNPROFOR, but on the other hand, British, in a way, paper, which was sent, and they have -- in paragraph 2, they have explained their views as far as the Mujahedin are concerned, about the two parts of it, et cetera, it belongs to the subject material, as such. But the document is really in value at least valid, and it is an UNPROFOR document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour Trechsel, this mark "BH," does it not mean "Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina"? This is a command for Bosnia-Herzegovina in Kiseljak, and it pertains to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, where was the UNPROFOR headquarters in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: For UNPROFOR, at Kiseljak. And for the British Battalion, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that we've clarified this point. General, I have five minutes or less --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your time is up. Now is the time for your last question, but your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one document and one question. 4D567, 4D567. You will see it on your screen. This is a schematic of Central Bosnia, with the situation in November 1993. It is marked on this document that by that moment, BiH Army units had captured the following towns: Fojnica, 6.000 Croats fled; Bugojno, 15.000 Croatians fled; Novi Travnik, 3.000 Croatians fled; Travnik, 25.000 Croats fled; the area south of Zenica, 12.000 Croats fled; Kakanj, 15.000 Croatians fled; and Vares, 9.000 Croats fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My question to you, General: Were those Croats expelled from that area? Did they flee because of a justifiable reason, or, alternatively, did they just leave that territory for no reason at all to resettle in Herzegovina or in another part of the world?

utterances.speaker: Filip Filipovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figures are really impressive. It is difficult to imagine that somebody would leave their homes without pressure, without crimes being committed nearby, without realisation that they no longer can survive there and maintain their presence, without the perspective that things may improve, knowing the ratio of power and what had gone on before, without their own state, because what was supposed to be the successor to Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, at that point boiled down to brute force and nothing else, so people had to leave their homes to go who knows where. This was the situation of both the Croats and the Muslims, and Serbs elsewhere, but nobody leaves their home of their own volition, or following a political call, or anything like that. You do not leave your home if your life is not threatened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, General. Your Honours, my time is up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question on the Mujahedin. Can you tell us in what respect the presence of these foreigners in the 7th Brigade may have played a part in the clashes between the HVO and the BH Army? And let me fine-tune my question. If the Mujahedin had not been present, would there have been as many clashes as that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't claim anything like that, and I don't blame only the Mujahedins. They did not wage a policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, rather, they weren't the only ones who -- well, let me put it this way: I don't think we should tie all evil to their name. They just brought in a psychological change. Their numbers could not have been held responsible for the things that were ascribed to them. They were a good unit, in the sense of having carrying out commanders' orders, and later on they were concentrated in the El Mujahid. They were in the 7th Muslim Brigade, of course. Now, the 7th Muslim Brigade did not as act as a whole. When you say "the 7th Muslim Brigade," you mean the whole brigade, but they acted in groups on a broad area. So one brigade would appear in Bugojno, Travnik, Dusina, Kiseljak, all over the place. So it wasn't one unit. Organisationally and in terms of logistics, it was in one place, specifically in Zenica, and later on I don't know whether it changed places, but it was a unit from which the necessary structure and resources were taken to help other people to realise their goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Alaburic, what's the matter? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask what happened to Judge Trechsel because we didn't see your head and we thought that something happened. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm still alive, though it may not sound it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in your view, talking of the Mujahedin, were they known within the HVO, within the military wing of the HVO? Were they spoken about in areas where there were soldiers? Did they instill fear as to their image and what they may have done? Did they have any impact on the civilian population so that the mere mention of them being there may cause people to flee? Did they have this kind of strength or force of psychological impact which may have led HVO units to behave in a specific way and may have led the civilians to be caught by fear, so that even if crimes were ascribed to Mujahedins, this would cause panic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The activities of the Mujahedin and their combat -- the value of their combat and fighting ability, but psychologically, too, this had an effect on the enemy; in this case, the HVO. Now, the knowledge that heads were rolling, heads were being cut off in certain places, and I knew the names of some of those people, these rituals, moving around the territory when we weren't in conflict, displaying their manner of dress, their shouts to battle, and so on, the "Allahu Akbar" cries, "Allah is great," and all the other slogans - I don't want to show you what these cries are like - but, anyway, it all had a morale effect on the population and on the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, this influence on the population and on the morale of soldiers, do you think that it could lead soldiers to behave abnormally, in a way that they would not have behaved if they had been confronted with traditional soldiers, but here these Mujahedin were not traditional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, certainly. In relation to the number of others, they were certainly -- they certainly brought something new; combat values, the BH Army. They were a sort of catalyst.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to react with respect to the translation. The witness said that they were yeast, that the literal word is "yeast."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that she said "catalyst."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness explain what he meant by that? Witness, what did you mean when you said -- when you used the word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me put it this way: Soup with salt and soup without salt. So it was this addition of salt. It was this additive that produced a new product, gave a new value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a former senior officer in the JNA, on the opposite side, or on the friendly side - I don't know how you want to put it - I mean within the BH Army, there were former colleagues of yours who were with you in the JNA. You even had very good relations with some of them. You mentioned the late Alagic, for example. So when you were talking with them, did they discuss the problem of the Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't talk to me about them, because militarily speaking, they weren't a problem to them. But I knew that with the population, the Muslim population, the locals, autoctonos population, that they were a problem to them because of their conduct and this imposition by force of Sharia Law or whatever else linked to their daily lives. And I've already mentioned marriages to under-age girls, to young girls, and that was a novelty in those areas. And then women who were wearing black, that wasn't the custom beforehand. So this was something that the local Muslims didn't agree with and there's no dilemma there. It was something new that was imposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw the constitutional text regarding the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where, in a very explicit fashion, there is mention of the three constitutive nations and mention of the religions, of the three religions; Catholics, Orthodox, and Muslims. I would like to know whether these Mujahedins were disturbing this constitutional balance that had been struck.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't upset the constitutional balance by their numbers, but they introduced something new which had not -- that the local population had not seen the likes of anything like that, because the Bosnian area was a European area, just like any other -- or Yugoslav area, and suddenly we had the advent of something that was not commensurate to the civilisation that the normal people there had known up until then. And this was imposed by force, where they were able to impose it. In Han Bila, for example, or in the area where they were first accommodated - it's a valley separate from the Lasva River Valley - well, the situation there was flagrant, and in the town of Travnik as well. I had never seen a woman wearing - what's it called? - completely black clothes. And not one; there were many of them like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak and his Defence team mentioned on several occasions the "Islamic Declaration," written by Alija Izetbegovic. They told us, in so many words, that Izetbegovic wanted to Islamise the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 11th of April - it was Easter 1993 - my people's flags were hoisted. And previously for Bajram, the whole of Travnik was green. So this Islamisation was very sudden, at least in the external marks and signs of it. It engulfed a large area. And Alija's declaration, dating back to the 1970s, unless I'm mistaken, for which he was sentenced to a term in prison by the system of the day, as far as I remember, but the fact remains that suddenly, in the broad masses of the population, something was changing, something had happened which had never happened before. So I can't die under a green flag, whereas it would have been an honour for me to have laid down my life under the tricolour flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have 10 minutes before the end of this hearing. Let me ask the Defence teams. They have two hours altogether. I would like to know who wants to take the floor first. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, or good evening, I should say, Mr. President and Your Honours, to everyone in and around the courtroom. We will not be cross-examining the gentleman, but we do wish to thank him for coming here to give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll skip -- no, we'll not skip 2D. Ms. Nozica, 2D.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We are going to cross-examine the witness, but I always insist upon our internal order, and by that order I'm third in line. We do intend to examine the witness. We know the amount of time we have at our disposal, and I think we're going to need around 30 minutes for our cross-examination. And if we exceed that time, then we'll ask to use our own time. But as far as I know, other Defence teams will be cross-examining this witness as well, so it will be a good idea for us to hear everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. 2D, 30 minutes. What about 3D, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence of General Praljak will be cross-examining this witness, and we will need half an hour. We think that we'll be able to conclude the cross-examination within that time. However, if there will be no cross-examination by other Defence teams, then we would, of course, like to use that additional time. We'd welcome it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For Mr. Coric, 5D?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the time being, we don't intend to cross-examine. However, based on experience, when new topics are broached, I would like to reserve the right to cross-examine within the two hours that have been allocated to the various Defence teams. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We probably won't be cross-examining this witness. And as we are reaching the end of today's day, we'll make the final decision tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we should start now. We only have a few minutes left. We will start tomorrow afternoon. We'll start with the two Defence teams who said they would take the floor, 2D and 3D. And then Mr. Scott will start, so he has to be ready with his binders for his own cross-examination. I wish you all a pleasant evening, and we will meet tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of December, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
